speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I read about the Wang Fuk Court tragedy in Hong Kong, Grenfell Tower in London, or even the Le Constellation bar fire in Switzerland just a couple of weeks ago, I think: these are world-class cities, cities with resources, cities with regulations, and yet, fire found a way.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To me, a fire feels different from other disasters.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It feels like it could actually happen to me.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would venture that many other Singaporeans feel the same.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While this may be a statistical blip, given the small numbers, it is a sobering reminder that fire remains an ever-present danger in our lives.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be clear, I believe that Singapore has strong fire safety standards.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats are designed as fire compartments to delay the spread of fire until help arrives.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) is well-trained and effective, and our fire codes and building codes are well thought out and comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But our good standards make continued vigilance all the more important.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad to hear that the Government has started a review of existing fire safety regulations governing building construction and maintenance work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must not limit ourselves to just the lessons from Wang Fuk Court, tragic as it was.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must also be cognisant of other hidden dangers, whether they are established practices that have become collective blind spots or new emerging risks that require novel approaches.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, today, I want to address three areas where I think we can close important gaps.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First is barriers to egress; second, battery fires we invite into our homes and third, the widening gap in fire safety standards across different generations of flats and estates.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 2.3.9(a) of the SCDF Fire Code stipulates that exit doors must be openable "without the use of a key, tool, or special knowledge" from the inside.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a panic, people fumble and seconds matter.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the standard we apply to shopping centres and offices is deemed optional for our own homes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is, of course, a deliberate policy choice.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the question is whether we should revisit it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For decades, our HDB flats came standard with a wrought iron gate secured by a double cylinder lock.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, that is sometimes known as a "key-to-key" lock, that is a lock that requires a key to open from either side.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, residents in these their flats do not need to fumble for a key to get out.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These gates are designed such that it is not easy for a prospective intruder to reach around the bars and operate the thumb turn from the outside.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, I think this is a very positive development, but it also means that millions of our flats still have legacy double cylinder locks.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For decades, concerns about intruders overrode the need for fire safety.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this sometimes comes at a heavy cost.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In August last year, a fire broke out in Jalan Bukit Merah.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A couple in their 30s were seen at the kitchen window shouting for help.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their neighbours crawled through smoke to reach them but were stopped by a locked entrance gate.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, this couple were found unconscious in the kitchen and later died in hospital.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will never know if the locked gate might have been the decisive factor in this case.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We often install big, chunky padlocks on our HDB gates.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, now, you have two locks, two keys and two points of failure.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a smoke-filled flat, fumbling for one key is difficult enough.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many households install these keyed grilles to prevent falls from height.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But over time, keys get lost, or the grilles are not even designed to be opened, to begin with, which means when firefighters arrive with a ladder, another potential exit is sealed shut.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what is slightly confounding to me is that we are hyper-cognisant of the threats to egress that are faced by new technologies.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We now require digital locks that are installed on fire-rated main doors to be certified, recognising that they pose a potential egress risk.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, for established practices like keyed gates, window grilles and other risks, we have normalised a clear safety deviance.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would also like to touch briefly on the Home Improvement Programme (HIP).

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, as part of the HIP, residents have the option to replace their old gates with a mild steel gate with an interior thumb-turn, so much like those that are installed on new BTOs.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is, we offer residents the option to replace an old gate that is a fire risk with a new gate that is also a fire risk!

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are subsidising the installation of new fire hazards in 2026.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not legacy infrastructure we are dealing with and managing, but a new risk that we are actively creating.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would seem, to me, that there is an easy path to addressing this risk.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, we should make the installation of new entrance gates with an interior thumb turn an "essential improvement" under the HIP scheme, fully subsidised and not optional.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Wrought iron gates with double cylinder locks should also be eliminated as an option.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Easy egress should be the default option and residents that prefer double cylinder locks for whatever reasons will have to make the choice to install it themselves.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also develop a phased replacement plan for legacy gates with double cylinder locks for estates that are not set to have an HIP exercise in the near future, prioritising older estates.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, we should incorporate the risks of keyed gates, additional padlocks and sealed window grilles into public education campaigns on fire safety.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second part of my speech will address battery fires.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we banned personal mobility devices (PMDs) from footpaths, many users simply migrated to modified mobility scooters instead.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new year has just begun and AMD fires are already making headlines.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just last Friday, four people were hospitalised in Tampines after a PMA fire.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for the fatal Bukit Merah fire I mentioned earlier, the SCDF findings indicate the blaze likely originated from a non-compliant PMD battery pack in the living room.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thermal runaway, which is a self-sustaining chemical reaction that releases toxic fumes and jet-like flames that breach fire compartments make them extra deadly.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intensity builds in seconds, giving residents little time to react, or fumble for a key.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Standard residential fire extinguishers are often useless as well.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We tell residents not to fight these fires themselves.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, we expect them to store, charge and manage these devices within their homes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On my estate walks, I have had several residents share their fear that their neighbours' AMDs being charged right by their front door, a ticking time bomb that might one day trap them within their own homes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not much can be done to assuage their fears, as today, as it stands, such charging practices are by and large permitted.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trying to enforce "compliant batteries" is futile when e-commerce makes cheap imports trivial.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The upcoming Land Transport and Related Matters Bill that was tabled today double styled on regulation but is unlikely to solve the enforcement gap.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our current approach relies on compliance when it is fundamentally an infrastructure problem.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Batteries charged in controlled, outdoor environments – this serves both safety and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Equip them with fire suppression, thermal monitoring and make them faster and cheaper than home-charging.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Create the incentive for residents to charge AMDs outside of the home.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And thirdly, I would suggest that we implement periodic inspections of AMDs, especially batteries, with enforced replacement timelines as batteries degrade and age.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think once sufficient infrastructure is built out and residents learn new habits, we might even consider that it would be viable to outlaw the charging of PMDs and PABs within homes, eliminating the risk entirely.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fire safety in Singapore varies by when your block was built.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Newer BTOs have fire-rated doors, thumb-turn gates and multiple redundant evacuation routes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older blocks sometimes have single-staircase designs, enclosed corridors that trap smoke and densely packed flats.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In July of last year, a fire broke out in Toa Payoh Lorong 8.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fire was so intensed that it shattered windows and spread vertically to the floor above.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Flames breached the very compartments that our flats are designed around.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Water could not be charged up to the affected floors.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Firefighters had to manually haul hoses up 10 storeys via the staircase.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Infrastructure does not just age, it degrades and testing regimes may not catch all failure modes between annual checks.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Block 229, the block in question, is a 25-storey point block with only a single staircase.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Residents trapped above the burning unit had to flee upwards to the 24th floor, because the single staircase near the fire became impassable.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some sheltered in place whilst black smoke seeped into their homes and others relied on neighbours for assistance.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Several fires in the last years were in blocks with similar single-staircase configurations, where the most direct escape route was compromised.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And here is the equity dimension: we have most of our elderly, least mobile residents living in buildings with older infrastructure and design standards from an earlier era.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those least able to move quickly in an emergency are those most likely to be living in such housing.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many rental blocks feature densely packed flats and enclosed corridors as well.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can do more to protect these residents and so here is what I propose.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We prioritise older estates and those with more elderly residents.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, we should roll out sprinkler systems in common areas of older blocks systematically, and not just as pilots.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prioritise blocks with enclosed corridors and densely packed units.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has built a strong fire safety system.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our SCDF is world-class and our fire codes are comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We continue to improve with each new development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I think that today, we have touched quite a bit on the topic of fire safety in our homes earlier in Question Time, as well as now during the Adjournment Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I agree that fire safety in our homes is an important topic, it is one that Singaporeans care deeply about and therefore, I thank the Member for his Adjournment Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I agree with the central theme of his Adjournment Motion, that we must continue to be vigilant with risks, especially as our living environments, technologies, lifestyles and our demographics change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Allow me to address his concerns in three parts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: First, the overall residential fire situation I mentioned earlier and approach towards fire safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Second, risks relating to AMDs; and third, our community efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I shared earlier during Question Time that the residential fire situation in Singapore is stable over the past five years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I raise a correction – the Member mentioned that there were eight fatalities in 2025, by August 2025.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We had six in the whole of 2025.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: In terms of Singapore's overall fire fatality rate, it remains one of the lowest internationally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It is something that we watch very carefully and this statistic is provided by a 2025 report by the International Association of Fire and Rescue Services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This means that the majority of fire incidents stem from human behaviour and practices, and are preventable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Of course, we know every fire is one too many, and every death is one too many.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Fires escalate very quickly, place lives at risk and can have devastating and long-lasting consequences to both the individual, their families and even their neighbours, and we must do our utmost to stay vigilant and minimise the risks – so in those regard, I agree with the Member.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The SCDF adopts a risk-based and pragmatic approach towards fire safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Fire safety in residential buildings begin with good fire safety design, supported by enforcement, early detection, early warning of fires, effective firefighting response and public preparedness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We need all the different layers to come together, working in concert to be able to effectively reduce the overall risk of fires.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: All residential buildings in Singapore are designed and built in accordance with the prevailing Fire Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: On this, our view is that we want to contain and keep the fire within the unit and that is how we mitigate risk at a systemic level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Based on statistics, based on what we have observed, based on the fires that have taken place in recent years, this fire compartmentalisation principle is effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The Member cited a few examples – the cases in Toa Payoh and Bukit Merah – the fires were indeed intense, but it was relatively contained within either that unit or within that floor or one floor above.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It did not spread as extensively and this is, in large regard, because of the compartmentalisation principle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The Member also mentioned locks, windows and these are important considerations, but I think the principle here that I would like to highlight is we often have to trade off practicality as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: In this regard, security is also something that I think Singaporeans will prioritise and value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: At the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), we often say low crime does not mean no crime, and I think it is important for us to also ensure that we afford residents, Singaporeans, their choice, in terms of what kinds of locks for their doors and windows will be.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And I think from SCDF's perspective, from MHA's perspective, the fire compartmentalisation principle is good enough for us to proceed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: In addition, we believe residents probably know how to exit their house in the quickest manner because it is an environment that they are very familiar with, and they get out every single day, multiple times a day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Having said so, the Fire Code is periodically updated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We continuously make sure that it is updated with the latest advances in building design, technologies, and also an evolving understanding of fire risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Additional provisions have been introduced over the years, such as adequate exit staircases to support swift evacuation, as well as fire engine access roads and rising mains to support SCDF's firefighting operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I think it is something that is very important to emphasise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We recognise that fire safety regulations must strike a balance, once again, between risk reduction, practicality and cost.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Fire Code provisions are most effectively implemented in new developments at the design stage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: It will be practically difficult to retrofit older buildings with newer building design requirements, such as widening the width of corridors, and I think the Member can appreciate why.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Even if feasible, it will cause significant disruption and cost to both taxpayers and residents, and therefore, we apply the Fire Code to developments at the point of approval.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Existing flats will be subjected to SCDF's strict regulatory oversight and inspections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: And we have done so, such as the installation of dry risers and the replacement of main entrance doors with fire-rated doors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We believe that is a much better way to keep units as well as the overall corridors and floors safe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This approach has served us well and allows us to strike a balance between providing a robust fire safety regime and practicality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The Member also touched on fire safety in older point blocks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Specifically on older point blocks, which is where I grew up in, so I feel for the point, especially acutely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: However, under the Fire Code, most residential buildings currently require two exit staircases to provide means of escape in case of evacuation – and that is valid for today's Fire Code for new projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The older point blocks require a single exit staircase as stipulated by the Fire Code then, and based on the risk analysis, we believe that is wearable because there are only a few units per floor, so the number of evacuees are much reduced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Also, from a practical perspective, adding a second staircase in many of these are simply not practical because of the layout.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I think more importantly, over the years, what HDB has also done is to carry out various programmes to improve fire safety in some of these older point blocks to bring them up to date with the Fire Code requirements at the point of upgrade, and we will keep doing that as a principle, where we can practically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Effective enforcement is also a necessary complement to a robust Fire Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: SCDF works very closely with the Town Councils and MCSTs to keep up with the inspection and enforcement regimes in our housing estates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The Member mentioned about the fire in Toa Payoh, where it was perceived, it was observed, that the dry risers may not be working as intended.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This is something that we are looking into, but the key here is, it is not that the Fire Code is not working, but that the testing and inspection regime may be something that the Member is suggesting we increase the frequency of.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Currently, we do have a regular annual inspection regime for these dry risers to make sure they are functional, but again, it is the practicality of striking a balance between how frequent we want to do it and making sure that it is operationally ready.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Of course, our objective is to make sure that it is ready every time, all the time, but we do need to strike a balance because of the number of flats around the island, and we do believe the current frequency of the inspection regime is adequate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: I have touched on strong fire safety design and on enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: In addition to that, what is useful is early detection and response measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Since 2018, HFADs have been mandatory in all new homes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: For existing homes, we have adopted a risk-calibrated, practical approach, and we have mandated it for homes which are carrying out fire safety related addition and alteration works.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Nonetheless, we strongly encourage all homeowners to install HFADs and homeowners can actually tap on the HIP and the Enhancement for Active Seniors programme to install HFADs at heavily subsidised rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: HFADs are fully funded for public rental flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Through the years, SCDF has continuously enhanced its firefighting capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Technologies, such as aerial appliances and surveillance drones, are a key enabler when deployed to tackle high-rise fires.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: However, I would like to highlight that residents can also play a part in firefighting response, prior to SCDF's arrival.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: To this end, we have improved access to firefighting equipment so that residents can better tackle minor fires.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Singaporeans would notice that we have fire extinguishers and AEDs installed in almost every other HDB block.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Hose reels and fire extinguishers are also available in common spaces such as coffee shops, car parks and roof gardens, as required under the Fire Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: While we continue to strengthen our collective response, we also regularly review the overall landscape for emerging risks of which one area of concern is indeed AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: AMDs have improved mobility and independence for many residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: However, their lithium-ion batteries pose fire risks and hazards that can result in AMD fires burning hotter and spreading more rapidly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: The risks are even higher with devices that do not comply with the relevant safety standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: That is why the Government takes a strict enforcement approach towards the import, sale and use of non-compliant AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Since June 2021, local retailers must seek the Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) approval for the import of Personal Mobility Devices and Power Assisted Bicycles, and these devices must be compliant with safety standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: LTA also conducts regular enforcement operations against non-compliant AMDs on public footpaths, as well as retailers selling non-compliant AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: This Bill makes it an offence to keep unsafe devices, such as non-UL2272 certified e-scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: At the same time, enforcement must be complemented by public awareness and education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: While the Government continues to review our policies, programmes and regulations constantly, the best defence against home fires is an informed and prepared public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: Only when everyone comes together and remains vigilant, will we be able to further bring down the incidence of fires.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Goh Pei Ming)
text: We will continue to work hand in hand with Singaporeans, with residents, to make our homes safe.
